o: An inner ear infection that causes a ringing sound
The perception of sound in the absence of an external acoustic source
A sensorineural hearing loss above 4 kHz
Intolerance of everyday sounds at normal loudness
0.e: Tinnitus is a phantom auditory perception: sound is heard with no external acoustic source. Intolerance of ordinary sounds is hyperacusis, a separate (though often co-existing) symptom.

0.q: What distinguishes objective tinnitus from subjective tinnitus?
o: It is louder than 40 dB SL on loudness matching
It arises from a real sound in the body, such as vascular flow or muscle clicks
It occurs only after noise exposure
0.e: Objective tinnitus has a physical sound source in the body (vascular, muscular, Eustachian tube) that can sometimes be heard by an examiner. Subjective tinnitus is heard only by the patient and is far more common.

0.q: According to the Jarach et al. (2022) meta-analysis, roughly what proportion of adults experience tinnitus?
0.e: The pooled adult prevalence of any tinnitus is about 14 %. Only about 2 % have severe, life-affecting tinnitus.

0.q: In many patients tinnitus persists after the auditory nerve has been surgically cut. Which idea does this finding best support?
o: Tinnitus is generated centrally after the loss of peripheral input
Tinnitus originates only in the outer hair cells
Tinnitus is a purely psychological symptom
0.e: Persistence after eighth-nerve section shows the percept is maintained in the central auditory pathway. The current model: reduced cochlear input triggers central changes that generate the sound.

0.q: Two adults have similar tinnitus loudness matches. One ignores it; the other cannot sleep and feels anxious. What best explains the difference?
o: A difference in the degree of middle-ear stiffness
Engagement of networks linking the auditory cortex to attention, emotion and memory
A higher tinnitus pitch in the distressed patient
0.e: Loudness correlates poorly with distress. Whether tinnitus becomes a problem depends on non-auditory attention, emotional (limbic) and memory networks, not on its acoustic properties.

1.q: Noise exposure, ageing and ototoxic drugs typically damage which structures first?
1.e: Outer hair cells are the most vulnerable and their loss accounts for thresholds up to about 50–60 dB HL. Inner hair cell loss usually follows with greater damage.

1.q: Cochlear synaptopathy mainly removes ribbon synapses on which type of auditory nerve fibre?
o: Low-spontaneous-rate type I fibres from inner hair cells
High-spontaneous-rate type II fibres from outer hair cells
Type II fibres from inner hair cells
1.e: Synaptopathy preferentially affects low-spontaneous-rate (high-threshold) type I fibres. These code sound in noise and at high levels, so thresholds can stay normal.

1.q: A 24-year-old DJ has tinnitus and a normal audiogram from 0.25 to 8 kHz. Which finding would best support hidden hearing loss (cochlear synaptopathy)?
o: Absent acoustic reflexes with a normal tympanogram
Reduced ABR wave I amplitude with normal thresholds
Prolonged ABR wave I–V interpeak latency
1.e: Loss of IHC synapses reduces the summed auditory nerve response, so ABR wave I amplitude falls while thresholds stay normal. Extended high-frequency thresholds are also often poorer.

1.q: Approximately what proportion of afferent auditory nerve fibres are type I fibres from inner hair cells?
1.e: About 95 % of afferent fibres are type I and synapse on inner hair cells. The remaining 5 % are type II fibres innervating outer hair cells.

1.q: A factory worker has a bilateral 4 kHz notch with recovery at 8 kHz. Where is his tinnitus pitch most likely to be matched?
1.e: Tinnitus pitch usually lies inside the region of hearing loss. In noise-induced hearing loss the match typically falls in the 3–6 kHz notch.

2.q: Which cell type in the dorsal cochlear nucleus is most implicated in tinnitus-related hyperactivity?
2.e: DCN fusiform (pyramidal) cells show increased spontaneous firing and synchrony after cochlear damage, and are also where somatosensory input converges.

2.q: Central gain after cochlear damage is mainly produced by which change?
o: Down-regulation of GABA and glycine inhibition with raised excitability
2.e: Homeostatic plasticity reduces GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition so central neurons restore average activity. This also amplifies spontaneous firing and synchrony, which can be perceived as sound.

2.q: Along the auditory pathway, which structure is the thalamic relay that shows raised spontaneous firing in tinnitus models?
2.e: The medial geniculate body is the auditory thalamus. Increased spontaneous activity is reported in the DCN, IC, MGB and auditory cortex. The lateral geniculate body is visual.

2.q: A patient with tinnitus also finds cutlery and traffic noise uncomfortably loud at normal levels. What mechanism links the two complaints?
o: Loss of the stapedius reflex arc
Retrocochlear compression of the cochlear nerve
2.e: The same increase in central gain that amplifies spontaneous activity also amplifies sound-evoked responses. This explains why tinnitus and hyperacusis frequently co-exist.

2.q: In the central gain model, where along the frequency axis is spontaneous hyperactivity greatest?
o: Within the hearing loss region and at its edge
Only at frequencies with normal thresholds
2.e: Hyperactivity is driven by lost input, so it peaks in the deprived region and at the edge of the audiogram where the input contrast is steepest.

3.q: How is primary auditory cortex on Heschl's gyrus tonotopically organised in humans?
o: High frequencies anterolateral, low frequencies posteromedial
Low frequencies anterolateral, high frequencies posteromedial
Low frequencies superior, high frequencies inferior
3.e: Heschl's gyrus maps low frequencies anterolaterally and high frequencies posteromedially.

3.q: After a high-frequency hearing loss, what happens to deprived neurons in the auditory cortex according to the map-reorganisation model?
o: They respond only to low-frequency sounds below 250 Hz
They start responding to the edge frequency of the audiogram
3.e: Deprived neurons shift their tuning towards the edge frequency, so the edge becomes over-represented and hyperactive (Eggermont & Roberts 2004).

3.q: A patient has normal hearing up to 2 kHz and a steep loss above. Which cortical frequency region does the map model predict will be over-represented?
3.e: The model predicts over-representation at the edge frequency of the loss, here near 2 kHz, as deprived high-frequency neurons take on edge tuning.

3.q: Which observation weakens the idea that tonotopic map reorganisation alone causes tinnitus?
o: Map changes also occur in people with hearing loss but no tinnitus
Heschl's gyrus has no tonotopic organisation
Tinnitus never occurs with high-frequency loss
Map changes are seen only in the cerebellum
3.e: Map changes are also found without tinnitus, so they are not sufficient on their own. The evidence linking reorganisation to tinnitus is mixed.

3.q: What does current evidence show for map-based sound therapies such as notched music or 'tailor-made' sound?
o: Stronger benefit than CBT for distress
Recommended first line by NICE NG155
3.e: Therapies targeting the map (notched music, tailor-made notched sound) have not shown consistent benefit in controlled trials and are not recommended as first-line treatment.

4.q: In Jastreboff's neurophysiological model, what makes tinnitus bothersome?
o: The loudness of the signal in the cochlea
Limbic and autonomic systems attach fear and alarm to the signal, forming a conditioned reflex
Middle-ear muscle spasm amplifying the sound
4.e: Jastreboff proposed that the signal becomes bothersome when limbic and autonomic systems link it to threat. This conditioned reflex keeps attention on the sound regardless of its loudness.

4.q: Thalamocortical dysrhythmia in tinnitus is characterised by which pattern of neural activity?
o: Alpha activity in the cochlear nucleus only
Increased beta in the motor cortex
Slow theta bursts in deprived thalamic neurons with gamma activity in surrounding cortex
4.e: Deprived thalamic neurons shift to low-threshold theta bursting, and surrounding cortex generates gamma activity that is thought to reflect the phantom percept.

4.q: In Rauschecker's (2010) noise-cancellation model, which structures normally gate the tinnitus signal?
o: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens, via the thalamic reticular nucleus
Superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus
Primary visual cortex and lateral geniculate body
4.e: The vmPFC and nucleus accumbens act through the thalamic reticular nucleus to suppress the unwanted signal. When this gating fails, tinnitus becomes chronic.

4.q: A patient with tinnitus reports anxiety, poor sleep and a racing heart when the sound is noticed. Which structure drives this autonomic stress response?
4.e: The hypothalamus drives the autonomic stress response in distressed tinnitus. Limbic structures (amygdala, insula, cingulate) supply the emotional load.

4.q: What is the main goal of counselling, CBT and tinnitus retraining therapy (TRT)?
o: Complete elimination of the tinnitus sound
Habituation, so the sound may remain but no longer matters
Permanent masking of the tinnitus by louder noise
4.e: These approaches aim for habituation of the reaction to and perception of tinnitus: the sound may still be present but stops capturing attention or causing distress.

5.q: Approximately what proportion of people with tinnitus can change its loudness or pitch with jaw, head or neck manoeuvres?
5.e: Somatic modulation is common: about 60–80 % of people with tinnitus can alter it with jaw clenching or head and neck movements.

5.q: Where do trigeminal and upper cervical somatosensory inputs converge with auditory input in the brainstem?
o: Fusiform cells of the dorsal cochlear nucleus
5.e: Trigeminal (via the spinal trigeminal nucleus) and C2 (via the cuneate nucleus) inputs converge on DCN fusiform cells, where they are up-regulated after hearing loss (Shore).

5.q: Upper cervical (C2) somatosensory input reaches the dorsal cochlear nucleus mainly through which relay?
5.e: C2 input relays through the cuneate nucleus, whereas trigeminal input relays through the spinal trigeminal nucleus. Both project to the DCN.

5.q: Tinnitus began after a whiplash injury, worsens with neck posture and comes with neck pain. Hearing is normal. Which management is most appropriate?
o: Oral steroids for sudden hearing loss
Assessment and physiotherapy for the cervical spine
5.e: This fits somatic tinnitus (Michiels 2018 criteria): onset after neck trauma with posture-related fluctuation and neck pain. Physiotherapy for the neck is the recommended management.

5.q: What does bimodal neuromodulation for tinnitus involve?
o: Pairing sound with electrical stimulation of the tongue or cheek and neck
Alternating left- and right-ear masking noise
Pairing hearing aids with a cochlear implant
5.e: Bimodal neuromodulation pairs sound with somatosensory (tongue or cheek-neck) stimulation to exploit auditory-somatosensory convergence in the DCN. It is an emerging option.

6.q: A patient hears a 'whooshing' sound in time with her heartbeat. What is the most likely category of cause?
6.e: Pulse-synchronous tinnitus means the ear is hearing blood flow. It usually has a vascular cause and always needs investigation.

6.q: Otoscopy in a patient with pulsatile tinnitus shows a red mass behind the intact tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
6.e: A red, pulsating retrotympanic mass with pulsatile tinnitus suggests a glomus (paraganglioma) tumour. Imaging and ENT referral are required.

6.q: A young woman with a raised BMI has headaches, transient visual blurring and pulsatile tinnitus. Which bedside examination is most important?
6.e: This picture suggests idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Fundoscopy for papilloedema is a key step in the pulsatile tinnitus work-up.

6.q: A patient reports irregular clicking in one ear. Tympanometry in extended-time mode shows rhythmic compliance changes synchronous with the clicks. What is the likely cause?
o: Middle-ear myoclonus of the stapedius or tensor tympani
6.e: Rhythmic contractions of the stapedius or tensor tympani cause clicking. They show up as rhythmic compliance changes on extended-time (reflex decay mode) tympanometry.

6.q: After major weight loss, a patient hears his own breathing and voice loudly in one ear; symptoms ease when lying down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
6.e: A patulous Eustachian tube stays open, causing autophony and breathing-synchronous roaring. It is linked with weight loss and eases when lying down; the drum may move with respiration.

7.q: A patient scores 46 on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory. Using the McCombe (2001) grading, how is this classified?
7.e: THI grades (McCombe 2001): 0–16 slight, 18–36 mild, 38–56 moderate, 58–76 severe, 78–100 catastrophic. A score of 46 is Grade 3, moderate.

7.q: When measuring residual inhibition, what stimulus is typically presented?
o: A pure tone at the tinnitus pitch for 5 s at threshold
Speech at the most comfortable level for 5 minutes
A click train at 90 dB nHL
Noise for 60 s at the minimum masking level plus 10 dB
7.e: Residual inhibition is tested by presenting noise for 60 s at MML + 10 dB, then recording whether and for how long the tinnitus is suppressed after the noise stops.

7.q: Tinnitus loudness matches in most patients are typically only about how loud?
7.e: Loudness matches are usually only 5–10 dB above threshold (SL), which is why they correlate poorly with the distress that questionnaires capture.

7.q: A patient has right-sided tinnitus. The right ear is 15–20 dB poorer than the left at 2 and 3 kHz, with poor speech discrimination. What is the appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and review in one year
Refer for MRI of the internal auditory meatus
Fit a sound generator and discharge
7.e: Unilateral tinnitus or asymmetric SNHL (≥ 15 dB at two adjacent frequencies) is a red flag for retrocochlear pathology such as vestibular schwannoma, and needs MRI of the IAM.

7.q: A man woke with new right tinnitus and a 70–90 dB HL right sensorineural loss that developed overnight. What is the correct action?
o: Routine hearing aid fitting in 3 months
Urgent same-day ENT referral for steroids and MRI
Pitch matching and a follow-up in 6 weeks
7.e: Sudden SNHL (≥ 30 dB over 3 contiguous frequencies within 72 h) is an otological emergency. Refer urgently for oral or intratympanic steroids and MRI.

8.q: Which intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing tinnitus-related distress and improving quality of life (Cochrane 2020)?
8.e: The 2020 Cochrane review found CBT reduces tinnitus distress and improves quality of life, although loudness changes little.

8.q: A patient with chronic tinnitus and no hearing loss asks for a tablet to cure it. What do AAO-HNS 2014 and NICE NG155 advise?
o: Start an anticonvulsant as first line
Do not routinely prescribe drugs for tinnitus itself; treat anxiety, depression or insomnia in their own right
8.e: Neither guideline recommends medication or supplements for tinnitus itself. Co-existing anxiety, depression and insomnia are treated on their own merits.

8.q: A 68-year-old with a bilateral sloping high-frequency loss has bothersome tinnitus and difficulty following conversation. What is the most appropriate first-line step?
o: Hearing aid evaluation with education and counselling
8.e: When hearing loss is present, hearing aids restore input in the deprived region and improve communication. AAO-HNS 2014 recommends a hearing aid evaluation alongside education and counselling.

8.q: Tinnitus retraining therapy (TRT) combines which components?
o: Complete masking with loud noise for 2 weeks
Directive counselling with low-level sound therapy for about 12–24 months
Antidepressants with hearing aids for 3 months
8.e: TRT pairs directive counselling based on Jastreboff's model with low-level sound (below the level that masks the tinnitus) over about 12–24 months. The evidence is moderate to low.

8.q: An adult with single-sided profound deafness has intrusive tinnitus in the deaf ear. Which intervention often reduces the tinnitus?
8.e: Cochlear implants often reduce tinnitus in single-sided or bilateral profound deafness by restoring auditory input to the deprived pathway.
